content: Positive use of norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol may sometimes indicate prodromal symptoms of a cerebrovascular event. Bleeding Irregularities Unscheduled Bleeding and Spotting Unscheduled (breakthrough) bleeding and spotting can occur in women using norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol. In cases of unscheduled bleeding, it is essential to consider non-hormonal causes and conduct appropriate diagnostic evaluations to rule out malignancy, other pathologies, or pregnancy, as is standard for any abnormal vaginal bleeding. If pathology and pregnancy are excluded, the bleeding may resolve with time or by switching to another contraceptive product. In clinical trials, most women experienced scheduled (withdrawal) bleeding starting on the fourth day of the drug-free interval, with a median duration of 5 to 6 days. On average, 26% of women per cycle experienced 7 or more total days of bleeding and/or spotting, including both scheduled and unscheduled events. Three clinical studies involving 3,330 women completing 22,155 cycles of norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol exposure assessed bleeding patterns. Approximately 1% of women discontinued the product, at least in part, due to bleeding or spotting. Amenorrhea and Oligomenorrhea In cases of amenorrhea, the possibility of pregnancy should be considered. If the patient has not adhered to the prescribed dosing schedule (e.g., missed a patch or started a patch late), pregnancy should be evaluated at the time of the first missed period, and appropriate diagnostic measures should be taken. If the patient has adhered to the regimen but misses two consecutive periods, pregnancy should be ruled out. Some women may experience amenorrhea or oligomenorrhea after discontinuing hormonal contraceptives, particularly if these conditions were pre-existing. Hormonal Contraceptive Use Before or During Early Pregnancy Extensive epidemiological studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects in women who used oral contraceptives before pregnancy. Additionally, studies do not suggest teratogenic effects, particularly concerning cardiac anomalies and limb reduction defects, when oral contraceptives are inadvertently taken during early pregnancy. If pregnancy is confirmed, norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol use should be discontinued. Combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) should not be used as a test for pregnancy. Depression Women with a history of depression should be carefully monitored. If depression recurs to a significant degree, norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol should be discontinued. Carcinoma of Breasts and Cervix Norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol is contraindicated in women with current or past breast cancer, as breast cancer may be hormonally sensitive. Substantial evidence indicates that CHCs do not increase the incidence of breast cancer. While some earlier studies suggested a potential increase in breast cancer risk with CHC use, more recent studies have not confirmed these findings. Some studies have associated combination oral contraceptive use with an increased risk of cervical cancer or intraepithelial neoplasia. However, the extent to which these findings are influenced by differences in sexual behavior and other factors remains controversial. Effect on Binding Globulins The estrogen component of CHCs may increase serum concentrations of thyroxine-binding globulin, sex hormone-binding globulin, and cortisol-binding globulin. This may necessitate an increased dose of replacement thyroid hormone or cortisol therapy. Monitoring Women using hormonal contraceptives should have an annual visit with their healthcare provider for a blood pressure check and other indicated healthcare evaluations. Hereditary Angioedema In women with hereditary angioedema, exogenous estrogens may induce or exacerbate symptoms of angioedema. Chloasma Chloasma may occasionally occur, particularly in women with a history of chloasma gravidarum. Women prone to chloasma should avoid sun or ultraviolet radiation exposure while using norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol. Adverse Reactions Clinical Trials Experience Serious adverse reactions associated with combination hormonal contraceptives, including norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol, include: Serious cardiovascular events and stroke. Venous and arterial thromboembolic events. Liver disease. Commonly reported adverse reactions include: Irregular uterine bleeding. Nausea. Breast tenderness. Headache. Adverse reaction rates observed in clinical trials may not directly compare to those in other trials or reflect rates in clinical practice. Data from 3,330 sexually active women (3,322 with safety data) in three Phase 3 clinical trials evaluating contraceptive efficacy and safety showed the following common adverse reactions (≥5%): breast symptoms, nausea/vomiting, headache, application site disorders, abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, menstrual disorders, and mood/anxiety disorders. The most common reasons for discontinuation were application site reactions, breast symptoms (e.g., discomfort, engorgement, pain), nausea/vomiting, headache, and emotional lability. Adverse reactions reported in 3.5% of norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol-treated subjects included: Gastrointestinal disorders: Abdominal distension. General disorders and administration site conditions: Fluid retention, malaise. Hepatobiliary disorders: Cholecystitis. Investigations: Increased blood pressure, lipid disorders. Musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders: Muscle spasms. Psychiatric disorders: Insomnia, decreased/increased libido. Reproductive system and breast disorders: Galactorrhea, genital discharge, premenstrual syndrome, uterine spasm, vaginal discharge, vulvovaginal dryness. Respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders: Pulmonary embolism. Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders: Chloasma, contact dermatitis, erythema, skin irritation. Postmarketing Experience Adverse reactions identified during post-approval use of norelgesteromin/ethinyl estradiol are reported voluntarily and may not reliably estimate frequency or establish a causal relationship to drug exposure.
